text: Two decades have to pass inside a little over two hours, and the film crosses them on haircuts, records and the shifting width of a father's tolerance. Jean-Marc Vallée puts five sons in one French Canadian household through the 1960s and into the 1970s, where privacy is scarce and approval is rationed by a man with settled opinions about what a son is. One of the five carries the picture. What presses on him is not a single crisis but a calendar — Mass, birthdays, his father's taste in music, the low continuous arithmetic of who is in favour this month — and the film lets that accumulate rather than announce itself. Vallée plays a good deal of it as comedy, which in certain households is the only register in which anything true can be said out loud.

A doctor arrives at the largest prison in Latin America carrying an AIDS prevention program and no authority at all. What Héctor Babenco builds from that is less a plot than a queue: men come to the clinic, sit down and talk, and each is given the time a case history takes. The source is Dráuzio Varella's account of his own years inside the Casa de Detenção de São Paulo, and the medical habit shows in the method — symptoms first, verdict never. At 145 minutes the crowding becomes the argument. Cells hold more men than they were drawn for, and the camera keeps finding the arrangements made to live in them anyway: the hierarchies, the debts, the trades, the visits. Nothing in the first hour behaves like a thriller. It behaves like rounds.

Two men with nothing to sell find that a sufficiently well-told lie is a form of income. João Grilo supplies the scheme and Chicó supplies the conviction, and between them they work a small town in the Brazilian Northeast by handing each mark whatever it is he already wanted to believe. Guel Arraes keeps this to 104 minutes and keeps the register broad: the shapes of the jokes are very old, the timing is not, and the speech of the region carries most of the film's music. Poverty is never explained here. It is simply the condition that makes cleverness the only currency two men like these can carry, and Arraes stays clear about the difference between being quick and being safe. Fantasy sits on the genre list, and it does not stay decorative.

On 12 June 2000 a gunman took a city bus in Rio de Janeiro, and the country watched it happen live, on every network at once. That is the awkward position José Padilha starts from: his central material was public before he ever touched it, seen by an audience already certain it understood the afternoon. The 118 minutes go where the broadcast could not — outside the cordon, into what the officers ringing the street were and were not trained to do, into the distance between a siege and its coverage. The passengers are inside the bus. The negotiation is on the pavement. The picture the country received was assembled somewhere between the two, by people with cameras who were also part of the event, and Padilha treats television as a participant rather than a source.

Tonho is handed the arithmetic before he is handed anything else: carry out the killing his father requires, and the years behind him will outnumber the days in front. April 1910, the interior is dry, and two families have been settling a debt in sons long enough that the sequence now runs without anyone choosing it. Walter Salles allows the situation ninety-five minutes and no exit. Most of the pressure falls on the household's daily labour, which is short of hands, and on Pacu, the younger brother, still small enough to ask why. Then a tiny travelling circus crosses the same badlands, bringing with it a few days of somewhere else, and the film's question sharpens: whether a young man raised inside a sequence can picture himself standing outside it.

The lunch is announced as an anniversary, and every person at the table has come to settle a different matter: which of them ends up with the mother. Mama Cora is nearly eighty and lives with the son who can least afford her, an arrangement families reach by never quite discussing it. Alejandro Doria stages the whole thing at household volume — everyone talking at once, nobody listening, grievances aired sideways under cover of hospitality. Eighty-seven minutes, mostly indoors, mostly at a table. The comedy lives in the gap between what these people say about duty and what any of them is prepared to do about it, and Doria neither narrows the gap nor apologises for finding it funny. Nobody is drawn as the villain, which is what makes the afternoon hard to leave.

Thirteen minutes is the whole running time, and a tomato gets most of it. Jorge Furtado follows one from the field to a supermarket shelf to a kitchen where it is judged not good enough, and then keeps following it past the bin, which is where a film about food usually stops and where this one starts. The chain is the argument. Every link has people standing at it — someone who grows, someone who sells, someone with money to buy — and then, at the far end, whoever is waiting for what money has finished with. A short film cannot digress, and Furtado does not: the sequence is laid out in order, item by item, and the order is what does the damage. The tone stays that of a manual. Everything else rests on that choice.

Three genres are listed for this film — documentary, drama, comedy — and it earns all of them by declining to say which parts of Winnipeg it made up. Guy Maddin was born in the city, which sits at the geographic dead centre of North America, and he treats the accident of birthplace as a licence rather than a duty: civic history, family history and outright invention run through the same narration at the same speed, with no seam offered. Eighty minutes, and most of it frozen. What holds it together is the voice, circling, insisting, correcting itself, returning to the same streets and the same rooms until the city stops being a place and starts being a habit of mind. Whether any given anecdote happened is a question the film has already declined to take.

The monster of this picture buries the town's dead for a living, which means nobody in it gets to avoid him. Zé do Caixão wants a son of a particular quality, and he has decided that the search for a suitable mother excuses whatever is done along the way; the film is organised around his appetite and hands him the camera rather than his victims. Eighty-three minutes and one small town are the entire apparatus. José Mojica Marins draws much of his effect from the undertaker's ordinary standing, a man everyone must deal with sooner or later, going about a trade nobody wants to look at closely. Fantasy sits on the genre list, though the film hardly needs it yet. He is frightening while he is still only a man with a plan.

Flor buries a husband who gave her pleasure and trouble in equal measure, and marries one who gives her an address and a standing. Bruno Barreto sets the two men against each other as household arrangements rather than as men to be judged: Vadinho was appetite, gambling and no money by Friday; Dr. Teodoro is order, respectability and a name that carries. Barreto gives it 117 minutes and declines to hurry the first marriage out of the way, so the widow's grief and her relief arrive in the same rooms. The comedy takes her side without pretending the choice was ever simple, and it is frank about appetite in a way that refuses to treat a widow's as scandal. Fantasy is on the genre list, and the arrangement it permits is the joke the picture has been building toward.

One family in this town sells the groceries and buries the dead, which puts them in the room for most of what happens to anybody. Claude Jutra films rural Quebec in winter, at Christmas, when the store is busiest and the roads are at their worst, and gives the watching to a boy on the edge of adolescence. Very little is announced. The adults drink, flirt, complain about work and conduct their business in front of a child they assume is not listening, and Jutra's method is to trust that the assumption is wrong. A hundred and five minutes, mostly interiors, mostly cold. What he is after is the particular hour in which a boy stops reading grown-ups as weather and starts reading them as people with reasons of their own.

The cast is a butcher, his wife, a waitress, a man who enjoys hurting people and the keeper of a flophouse, and the film grants none of them standing above the others. Cláudio Assis works in Recife, in rooms that hold heat, cutting between these lives until proximity does the plotting; nobody here chooses to be involved with anybody, they are simply within reach. The butcher's trade is not incidental. Flesh is handled as goods in one place and handled no more gently in the next, and Assis lets the rhyme sit there without underlining it. There is no one here to root for, and Assis makes no attempt to supply one. The hundred and three minutes go instead to what a city does to people who cannot afford to walk out of a room, and to how ordinary cruelty becomes when nobody has anywhere else to be.

Two years on, the undertaker has an assistant, twenty-five more minutes of screen time and no intention of revising the plan. Zé do Caixão is still after the woman who will bear the child he believes the world owes him, and José Mojica Marins escalates by widening the operation rather than deepening the man: what was one figure's private cruelty in a small town is now staffed and organised. The horror turns procedural. Marins works out who assists, who is told what, and how a town accommodates someone it needs, and the flatness of that accounting is harder to sit with than any single act inside it. The first film could be watched as a village story. This one is a campaign, and 108 minutes is long enough for the change of scale to be felt.

The hero arrives fully grown, an adult delivered into a hut in the forest, and nobody in the film finds this worth remarking on. That is the register Joaquim Pedro de Andrade holds for a hundred and ten minutes: a rhapsody played without wonder, in which a magical change of skin and a change of address are given exactly the same weight. Macunaíma leaves the village for São Paulo and takes to the city as a dandy, an appetite with clothes on, borrowing whatever manners are required and dropping them at the door. The comedy is loose-limbed and deliberately coarse. Underneath it the film follows a man who becomes whatever the room in front of him rewards, and keeps careful count of what is left of him when the room empties.
